title: Ming Builders Put Sticky Rice in Their Mortar — But It's No Miracle | China Travel Expert
description:
You've probably heard that sticky rice is the secret that makes China's old walls unbreakable. Here's the honest version. In 2010, chemists at Zhejiang University analysed mortar from a roughly 600-year-old Ming city wall and found the real recipe: slaked lime mixed with sticky-rice soup. The rice's amylopectin controls how the lime's calcium-carbonate crystals grow, giving a finer, denser, more water-resistant mortar that shrinks and cracks less over centuries.

But "stronger than modern cement"? No. Researchers describe its raw strength as only average — the magic is in durability and crack control, not brute strength. It's clever ancient chemistry, not a super-glue. This short is a code-drawn diagram (no AI imagery), opening and closing on a real shot of Nanjing's Ming-era Zhongshan Gate.

🧭 Expert Tip: You can still see sticky-rice mortar doing its job on the Ming walls of Nanjing and Xi'an — look closely at the fine, pale joints between the big grey bricks.

糯米灰浆真有，但不是“比水泥还强”：浙江大学 2010 年研究发现，糯米中的支链淀粉让石灰结晶更细密、更抗水、更不易开裂——强度只算“一般”，耐久才是关键。
